title: The daily read: a five-minute routine, and the traps
hook:
Before every flight, an airline pilot with twenty years in the cockpit still runs the same checklist, item by item, in the same order. Not because they forget how to fly. Because when everything is checked the same way every time, the one thing that is different jumps out.

Reading markets works the same way. A busy morning throws a hundred headlines at you: a tanker incident, a Fed speech, an FII number, a rupee wobble, a broker's note on cement. Read them in whatever order they arrive and every day feels like a new story. Read them through a fixed set of questions and most days turn out to be the same story with small edits, and the rare day when the story actually changes becomes impossible to miss.

That is what this page is built for. The daily brief answers the same questions in the same order every morning. This chapter is the drill: what to look at, in what order, what it means, and the traps that catch even experienced investors.
short: Read the brief as a list of changes, not a newspaper: if the one-line verdict has not changed, the rest of the page is confirmation.
Of the four lights, oil, US rates and the dollar, flows and positioning, and the RBI, a light changing colour is the event; its level is just context.
Judge every move against that series' own normal wiggle. A small move in a pinned rupee can matter more than a big day for the Nifty.

Avoid the classic traps: one day of flows, an expected decision treated as news, a level mistaken for a change, too much faith in small historical tables, and the folklore that a crowded foreign short means a rally is coming.

sections.heading: Minute one: has the story changed?
sections.html:
Start at the top, with the verdict: the one-line state of play. Something like: a supply-led oil shock, the RBI defending the rupee, domestic money cushioning foreign selling.

Ask exactly one question. Is today's line different from yesterday's? Most days it is not, and that is useful information in itself. It means whatever the market did overnight, however loud the headlines, nothing has changed the underlying mechanism. The rest of the page then confirms what you already know, and your job is to resist inventing a new story out of noise.

On the rare day the verdict does change, stop and read properly. A shift from a currency defence to the RBI letting the rupee go, or from a grinding squeeze to a route reopening, changes which sectors win and lose. Those are the days that pay for the habit.

sections.heading: Minutes two and three: the four lights
sections.html:
Next come the four lights, one for each force that moves Indian stocks as a group.

  • Oil. The tax on India. Is the move supply-led or demand-led, and is the route through the Gulf open?
  • US rates and the dollar. The world's hurdle rate. Rising US yields and a strong dollar pull foreign money out and press on rich valuations.
  • Flows and positioning. The tug of war between foreign sellers and domestic buyers, and how foreigners are placed in futures.
  • The RBI. The price of money, the quantity of money and the price of the rupee, which in a crisis become one decision.

Here's the rule that matters most: a light changing colour is the event; the level is context. Oil has been high for months, and a high oil price on its own tells you nothing new today. Oil turning from red to amber, because tankers are moving again, is news. Think of a cricket scoreboard. A big total is context. A wicket falling is the event.

Each light points to a chapter. If one changes and you are not sure why it matters, that chapter is your next read.

sections.heading: Minute four: what moved more than it should have
sections.html:
The unusual-moves list ranks the day's changes against each series' own normal volatility, not by the raw size of the move. That sounds technical, but the idea is simple. A quiet colleague raising their voice tells you more than a loud one shouting again.

So a small move in the rupee, which the RBI has been holding nearly flat, can rank above a big day for the Nifty, because for the rupee it is far outside the usual range. It might mean the defence is being tested, or eased. That is worth knowing before the newspapers notice.

Each unusual move also lists the industries it tends to help or hurt, drawn from the industry pages. A jump in oil flags airlines, paints and fuel retailers; a jump in US yields flags richly valued IT and asset managers.

Then look at the winners and losers map: the sector tilt implied by the current regime and the house view. Hold it up against your own portfolio. If most of your money sits in the sectors the regime punishes, that is not a reason to trade today. It is a reason to know why you are holding them.

sections.heading: Minute five: what is coming, and what is expected
sections.html:
The last block lists the releases and meetings that could change a light: the inflation and industrial output prints, the RBI's policy meetings, Fed decisions, OPEC+ meetings, monthly fund-flow data, and the Budget when it is near.

For each one, know what the market expects before it happens. Markets move on the gap between what was expected and what arrived, not on the number itself. An RBI hike that everyone saw coming can lift stocks if the statement sounds softer than feared. An inflation print that rises less than forecast can be good news even though inflation went up.

That is the whole daily routine: the verdict, the lights, the outliers, your book, the calendar. Five minutes on a normal day.

sections.heading: The weekly and monthly layer
sections.html:
Some signals are too slow or too noisy to read daily. Give them a fixed slot instead.

  • Weekly. Read the hot spots chapter, the one part of the framework refreshed every week, for which conflicts are escalating and through which channel. Look at foreign flows over the whole week rather than day by day, and at the trend in the US ten-year.
  • Monthly. Domestic fund inflows, the floor under the market. Inflation, especially whether it is broadening beyond food and fuel into core. Industrial output, which with inflation decides the regime. And the government's capex spending, the quiet line that gets cut when budgets are squeezed.
  • Each RBI meeting. The vote split, the stance and the liquidity paragraph, not just the repo rate.

The daily read tells you what changed. The weekly and monthly layer tells you whether it is building into something.

sections.heading: Five traps that catch professionals too
sections.html:
1. Reading a single day of flows. One day's FII number can be swung by one large block deal or an index rebalancing. A month of selling is a signal; a day is an anecdote.
  2. Treating an expected decision as news. If everyone knew the RBI would hike, the hike is not the news. The wording is.
  3. Confusing a level with a change. High oil, a weak rupee, heavy foreign selling: all may be old news, already in prices. Ask what moved, not what is high.
  4. Over-fitting the regime and oil tables. They rest on a handful of episodes. Treat them as priors with weak statistics that tilt your thinking, never as rules that decide it.
  5. Trading folklore. Traders love to say a crowded foreign short must end in a short-covering rally. Our own data since 2022 says it has not reliably done so. Positioning tells you the mood, not the timing.
Ask what moved, not what is high.

sowhat:
The brief is a monitoring tool, not a trading signal. It will not tell you what to buy. Its job is narrower and more useful: to tell you which chapter's mechanism is driving the market this week.

  • If oil is the light that changed, reread the oil and Gulf chapter and the oil and rupee chain, and check your exposure to oil users.
  • If US yields moved, reread the dollar and US rates chapter, and look at your most richly valued holdings.
  • If the RBI moved, reread the RBI chapter, and check your lenders' funding.
  • If flows shifted, look at the monthly domestic data before reacting to the daily one.

When nothing has changed, the right action is usually none. The routine is what lets you tell the difference.
